title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137)
hookLine: exiles weep and hang up their harps; the psalm even holds their rage honestly

lines: A SONG ON THE DANCE FLOOR.
SING US A SONG OF ZION.
cards: A reggae song built from this psalm, and later a disco version, put it on dance floors. People dance to it at weddings and roller rinks, singing about sitting down by the rivers of Babylon.
The words are far older than the beat, and the psalm ends somewhere no party goes. Go back to the days after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonian army has burned the city and its temple.
Its people have been marched east, to the rivers and canals of Babylon. And their captors, in a cruel joke, ask them to sing.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof."

teach.h: SING US ONE OF THE SONGS OF ZION
teach.b: Then the cruelty: "For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion."
And the answer is the question at the center of the psalm: "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?" They won't perform their grief for the people who caused it.

teach.h: IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM
teach.b: Then a vow: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Cunning means skill. A harpist's right hand.
Let me never play again if I forget home. Now the hard part.

teach.h: RAGE KEPT IN THE TEXT, HONESTLY
teach.b: The last three verses turn to rage. They call down judgment on Edom, which cheered the destruction, and on Babylon, and the very last verse blesses whoever would dash Babylon's little ones against the stones.
It is hard to hear. And it's in the Bible. Christians have handled it in different ways.
Some churches leave those verses out when the psalm is prayed aloud.

teach.h: HOW SHALL WE SING THE LORD'S SONG IN A STRANGE LAND?
teach.b: Augustine and other early writers read the little ones as small evil thoughts, to be dashed against the rock, which they took to be Christ.
Other readers see the psalm as honest rage handed over to God in words, instead of acted out in the world. What the psalm doesn't do is pretend.
The Bible keeps the tears, the vow and the fury of people who lost everything.

how: Christians pray Psalm 137 in times of exile, grief and injustice; some churches omit its final verses in public worship, while others pray it whole as an honest lament.

o: the land of rivers where the exiles wept
the desert the exiles crossed going home
the hill country where Jerusalem stood

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the exiles happily sang for their captors
they hung up their harps: "how shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?"
the psalm ends with gentle words of comfort
it ends in raw rage against Babylon, which churches read and use in different ways.
Augustine read the psalm's little ones as small evil thoughts
he and other early writers read them as sins to be dashed against the rock, Christ.

games.q: you've been dragged far from your burned city. your captors laugh and say: sing us one of your songs from home. what do you do?
o: hang up your harp and refuse.
sing a song from their country instead.
games.why: "we hanged our harps upon the willows." they won't perform their grief for the people who caused it.

practice: Think of people who are where they never chose to be: refugees in camps, families split across borders, a neighbor who moved here and still cooks food that smells like somewhere else.
If you pray, hold them before God, by name or simply as they are; if you don't, hold them in mind with care, and let yourself feel a little of what they've lost.

wordCard.voice: Mesopotamia. The land of rivers and canals where the exiles sat down, wept, and refused to sing for their captors.

orig.note: Hebrew: the rivers of Babylon, the great rivers and canals of Mesopotamia.

carryVoice: Your line: how can we sing here? Some grief isn't for performing. Day four hundred thirty-seven.
